title: Morning Edition
notes: Morning Edition for Monday, Nov 23, 2026. There was no edition on Sunday, Nov 22; this edition covers news since the Nov 21 morning edition.

Leading this morning: the collapse of the COP31 climate talks, Democrats’ biggest House majority since 1992, Ukraine’s claimed sinking of a Russian warship in Libya, Montreal’s trade for Dylan Larkin, Hong Kong’s Election Committee race and a death sentence for a Chinese official convicted of spying. Also: an ICE arrest on a Seattle jet bridge, the Army’s plan to detonate explosives in Iowa, Tarik Skubal’s record Mets deal, Thanksgiving prices, Nova Scotia’s new Liberal leader, the Senate fight over Bill C-22, a study on daily cannabis use, the Parliamentary Press Gallery dinner, Hong Kong’s Interpol drone ban, Hong Kong winners at the Golden Horse Awards, a cancelled Tai Po fire book launch, a closing 90-year-old saucemaker, Beijing’s response to an FCC phone-number rule, BYD’s Ti7 ruling, a reported SEC inquiry into Nvidia, Kenya and DR Congo restoring ties, South Korea’s education minister resigning and Carlos Alcaraz’s ATP Finals win.

Updates on earlier stories: COP31 (overtime talks, Nov 21 edition; now collapsed without a deal); Nvidia and chips to China (California subpoena, Nov 21; now a reported SEC inquiry); the Tai Po fire (building-safety penalties, Nov 21; now anniversary events); the U.S. midterms (House count now near final).

Planned or scheduled, not confirmed when this edition was prepared: the Army’s Iowa detonation (Wednesday, Nov. 25), the Senate committee’s clause-by-clause review of Bill C-22 (Tuesday, Nov. 24), Hong Kong’s Interpol restrictions (Nov. 30–Dec. 3), the expected MLB lockout and the finalising of Skubal’s contract after a physical.

Photos appear on the lead and on 20 of 23 other stories. All are file photos; the COP31 photo was taken at the talks on Nov. 21, before they collapsed. Text-only where no suitable openly licensed photo was found: the Iowa detonation, the Chinese spy case, the FCC phone-number rule.

Stories by region: U.S. 5, Canada 5, Hong Kong 5, China 4, World 5. China has four stories: a fifth candidate (China–Singapore trade talks) mostly predated the last edition and rested largely on official and state-media accounts, so it was left out rather than padding the section. Several stories rest on a single outlet; this is noted under each story’s sources. Zelensky’s account of the Libya strike, the Iowa danger assessment and the Seattle assault accusation are claims or allegations, not established facts.
provenance: Compiled from the linked reporting, official releases and documents listed under each story; labels show whether a point is reported, an official statement, a claim, an allegation or analysis.

Source pages were opened during this morning’s research between about 6:27 AM and 6:39 AM ET on Nov 23; each check time is the logged time that page was fetched. Photo licences were read from each Wikimedia Commons file page’s metadata at the same session.

RTHK is Hong Kong’s government-funded broadcaster; Xinhua is Chinese state media; Focus Taiwan is the English service of Taiwan’s state-funded Central News Agency. Wire copy carried by another outlet is marked with the agency’s name (AP, AFP, The Canadian Press).

Access limits: AP’s own pages returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so AP reporting is cited via CBC and CBS; the South China Morning Post was not used because it blocks automated fetches; New York Times and Wall Street Journal originals on Nvidia are paywalled and were not opened. These are access limits, not evidence of errors.

Figures or details differ between sources on when the U.S. government’s Iowa court filing was made (Saturday vs Sunday) and on Alcaraz’s injury break (about four months vs four and a half); both are noted where relevant.

stories.headline: COP31 climate talks collapse without a deal after the final text left out any mention of fossil fuels
stories.deck: The longest UN climate summit on record ended in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday, Nov. 22, with no main political agreement, the first such collapse since Copenhagen in 2009.
stories.summary: The longest UN climate summit on record ended in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday, Nov. 22, with no main political agreement, the first such collapse since Copenhagen in 2009. Talks were due to finish on Friday but ran into Sunday. A last-minute draft presented early Sunday did not contain the words “fossil fuels” at all; an earlier draft had mentioned them six times, which oil producers rejected, the BBC reported. The European Union, speaking through Irish minister Darragh O’Brien and EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra, refused to endorse a text that “does not even mention fossil fuels”, and Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu and others also objected. Poorer countries also complained that the text set no concrete figures for adaptation finance. Saudi Arabia’s delegate said Arab states had negotiated in good faith; Turkey’s COP31 president Murat Kurum said “there will be no new text”. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed”. Some side agreements survived: progress on a “just transition” mechanism, and more than 80 countries backed a target for electricity to meet 35% of global energy use by 2035. On Monday, Nov. 23, China’s foreign ministry called the outcome disappointing but said the green transition is “irreversible”.
stories.why: COPs work by consensus, so a handful of oil producers can block language the majority wants, and this time the majority refused to accept a weaker deal rather than paper over the split. The failure does not cancel the Paris Agreement or countries’ own plans, but it leaves no new global signal on fossil fuels or money for climate-hit countries just as the world is expected to pass 1.5C of warming. Expect pressure to reform how COPs make decisions.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement
stories.note: Updates the Nov 21 edition, which reported the talks running past their Friday deadline. The 35%-electrification goal (which China backed, Nov 21 edition) is a voluntary target, not part of a binding deal. China’s reaction comes from RTHK’s agency-based report of a foreign ministry briefing.

stories.headline: Democrats reach at least 258 House seats, their biggest majority since 1992, as Virginia Foxx concedes after a recount
stories.deck: Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx conceded North Carolina’s 5th District to Democrat Chuck Hubbard on Sunday, Nov. 22, after a recount left him 330 votes ahead.
stories.summary: Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx conceded North Carolina’s 5th District to Democrat Chuck Hubbard on Sunday, Nov. 22, after a recount left him 330 votes ahead. The machine recount netted Foxx one vote, NC Newsline reported. Foxx, 83, had held the seat since 2005; Hubbard, a former journalist, lost to her in 2024. With the result, Democrats have won at least 258 House seats to Republicans’ at least 173, with four races uncalled, the BBC reported, the most for either party since 1992. North Carolina’s delegation flips from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to 11 Democrats and three Republicans. “The peaceful transition of elected office from one person to another is one of the true hallmarks of our system of government,” Foxx said in her statement. Hubbard said he wanted to hold President Trump accountable and focus on the cost of living.
stories.why: A majority this large gives Democrats room to pass their own bills through the House and to run investigations of the administration from January without relying on every member. It also shows how far the cost-of-living backlash reached: districts like this one in north-western North Carolina were considered safely Republican.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement
stories.note: Final seat totals were not settled when sources were checked; four House races were still uncalled per the BBC.

stories.headline: Masked ICE officers arrest a father and daughter on a Seattle airport jet bridge, drawing outrage from the airport and Washington’s governor
stories.deck: Immigration officers detained two Mexican nationals as they boarded Alaska Airlines Flight 1306 to Los Angeles at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning, Nov. 21.
stories.summary: Immigration officers detained two Mexican nationals as they boarded Alaska Airlines Flight 1306 to Los Angeles at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning, Nov. 21. The Department of Homeland Security said Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza had overstayed his visa and that his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, “hurled hot coffee” at officers and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer. Their lawyer, Olia Catala, said they have no criminal record, that the father has a pending asylum claim and that the coffee was knocked from her hand when plain-clothes, masked officers lunged; an eyewitness told Reuters he did not see anyone throw coffee. The Port of Seattle, which runs the airport, said it was “outraged” and was asking whether agreed protocols were breached; Alaska Airlines said it had no advance notice, and the flight left more than two hours late with a new crew, CBS reported. Gov. Bob Ferguson called ICE “completely and totally out of control.” The two were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, their lawyer said.
stories.why: Airports are where many immigrants with pending cases travel openly on their documents, so arrests at the gate spread fear well beyond this family. The clash between a federal agency and the local airport operator, and the dispute over the coffee, will matter in court: an assault charge can decide whether someone gets bond.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Allegation
stories.note: The assault accusation is DHS’s allegation and is disputed by the family’s lawyer and an eyewitness; no charge outcome is known. The wire quote from the eyewitness is via the BBC.

stories.headline: Army plans to detonate nearly five tonnes of unstable lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday despite a court pause, citing an emergency exemption
stories.deck: The Justice Department told a federal appeals court the Army will invoke an emergency exception to environmental rules to blow up degraded explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown.
stories.summary: The Justice Department told a federal appeals court the Army will invoke an emergency exception to environmental rules to blow up degraded explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown. The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had paused the Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency permit after environmental groups sued, saying lead dust could travel far and safer options were not considered. Government lawyers argued that the roughly 9,700 pounds of lead azide in 68 barrels has formed unstable crystals and could “spontaneously explode” as temperatures drop below freezing, and that “a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion”. The filing said the Army would act by Tuesday, Nov. 24; on Sunday evening the Army said it now plans the detonation for Wednesday, Nov. 25, “to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced”. Earthjustice, representing the groups, argues the move would bypass the court.
stories.why: This is a test of how far the government can go around a court order by declaring an emergency. Residents face a real dilemma: an uncontrolled blast would be worse, but lead is toxic and families near the plant were given little notice. Watch whether the court responds before Wednesday.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Claim
stories.note: Planned, not confirmed: the detonation had not happened when sources were checked. Sources differ on when the government’s filing was made (late Saturday per the BBC and Al Jazeera; ABC says Sunday) and on whether the court’s pause came Thursday night or Friday. The danger assessment is the government’s claim in court.

stories.headline: Tarik Skubal agrees to a record $450 million, nine-year deal with the New York Mets, sources say
stories.deck: The two-time Cy Young winner’s contract would be the largest ever for a pitcher, according to people familiar with the deal; the Mets have not confirmed it pending a physical.
stories.summary: The two-time Cy Young winner’s contract would be the largest ever for a pitcher, according to people familiar with the deal; the Mets have not confirmed it pending a physical. The reported terms, first emerging on Sunday, Nov. 22, average $50 million a year, topping Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s $325 million Dodgers deal, and include a full no-trade clause, no opt-outs, a $45 million signing bonus and $30 million in deferred pay. Only Juan Soto, Shohei Ohtani and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. have bigger contracts. Skubal, a left-hander who turned 30 on Nov. 20, joins a Mets team that finished last in the NL East at 74-88 despite baseball’s highest payroll; the Toronto Blue Jays were among the teams that met him. The deal comes about a week before owners are expected to lock players out in a labour fight over the owners’ push for a salary cap.
stories.why: For New York fans it is a statement that the Mets will keep spending after a bad season. For the sport, it lands days before a possible lockout: a contract this size is exactly what owners want a salary cap to stop, and what the players’ union wants to protect.
stories.label: Reported + Unnamed sources

stories.headline: A classic Thanksgiving dinner for 10 costs about 6% more this year, Farm Bureau survey says, led by pricier turkey
stories.deck: The American Farm Bureau Federation puts the average cost at $58.63, or about $5.86 a person, the first rise since the 2022 record, though another estimate expects deals to keep food bills slightly lower.
stories.summary: The American Farm Bureau Federation puts the average cost at $58.63, or about $5.86 a person, the first rise since the 2022 record, though another estimate expects deals to keep food bills slightly lower. A 16-pound frozen turkey averaged $23.68, up 10%, with cranberries, whole milk and dinner rolls also up, while veggie trays, pie crusts, peas and whipping cream fell; the group blamed high diesel costs and farm labour shortages. Volunteers checked prices in the first week of November, and stores often cut turkey prices closer to the holiday. NPR reported on Monday, Nov. 23, that the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute expects the average Thanksgiving food bill to come in slightly cheaper than last year thanks to promotions, and that in a LendingTree survey 53% of people said inflation was affecting their holiday plans, with fewer planning to host.
stories.why: Thanksgiving prices are a small but very visible measure of the cost-of-living squeeze that dominated the midterms. The gap between the two estimates is a reminder that how you shop, sales and store brands, can matter as much as the headline number.
stories.label: Industry figures + Reported
stories.note: The Farm Bureau survey is informal and its menu has not changed since 1986; it was released Nov. 18 and is included here as background to NPR’s Nov. 23 report.

stories.headline: Canadiens land Dylan Larkin from the Red Wings in a blockbuster trade for Dach, Montembeault, Hage and two first-round picks
stories.deck: Montreal acquired the former Detroit captain on Sunday, Nov. 22, ending a saga that began when Larkin asked for a trade in the off-season.
stories.summary: Montreal acquired the former Detroit captain on Sunday, Nov. 22, ending a saga that began when Larkin asked for a trade in the off-season. The Canadiens sent forward Kirby Dach, goalie Samuel Montembeault, the rights to top prospect Michael Hage, first-round picks in 2027 and 2029, a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fourth-round pick; Montreal also got Detroit’s 2027 third-round and 2028 second-round picks, the team said. Larkin, 30, has 278 goals and 649 points in 818 games for Detroit, ranks 10th in team history in both, and has scored at least 30 goals in each of the last five seasons; he won Olympic gold with the United States at Milano-Cortina in 2026. CBC said he slots in behind Nick Suzuki as the second-line centre Montreal has wanted for more than a year.
stories.why: Montreal has been rebuilding around young players; paying this much in prospects and picks for a 30-year-old centre signals the Canadiens think they can contend now. For Detroit, it ends an awkward standoff with a franchise player and restocks its pipeline.

stories.headline: Former Tory minister Becky Druhan wins the Nova Scotia Liberal leadership, the first woman to lead the party
stories.deck: Druhan, who quit Premier Tim Houston’s Progressive Conservative cabinet and caucus in 2025, beat Richmond County councillor Amanda Mombourquette with about 68% of the points on Saturday, Nov. 21.
stories.summary: Druhan, who quit Premier Tim Houston’s Progressive Conservative cabinet and caucus in 2025, beat Richmond County councillor Amanda Mombourquette with about 68% of the points on Saturday, Nov. 21. The result was announced at a convention in Halifax. Almost 2,900 people voted, down from about 3,400 registered in the party’s 2022 race. Druhan, the MLA for Lunenburg West, served as education and justice minister before leaving over what she called a difference in values, sat as an Independent and joined the Liberals in May. The party has been without a permanent leader since the 2024 election cut it to two seats and the NDP became the official Opposition. “I hope that somewhere in Nova Scotia tonight, a young girl sees one more example of what’s possible for her, too,” Druhan said, adding the party would operate “as if the writ could drop at any moment”, since Nova Scotia has no fixed election date.
stories.why: Nova Scotia’s Liberals were nearly wiped out in 2024. Choosing a former Houston minister is a bet that someone who knows the government from inside can win back centrist voters, but she first has to rebuild a party that currently has three seats.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Big tech and police make final pitches as the Senate weighs Ottawa’s lawful-access bill, C-22
stories.deck: A Senate committee hears more witnesses on Monday, Nov. 23, and is scheduled to go through the bill clause by clause on Tuesday, CBC reports.
stories.summary: A Senate committee hears more witnesses on Monday, Nov. 23, and is scheduled to go through the bill clause by clause on Tuesday, CBC reports. Bill C-22 would give police and CSIS faster access to electronic data in investigations and could compel tech companies to adapt their systems to preserve and hand over information under warrant. After a backlash, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree amended it so providers would not have to decrypt data unless they supplied the encryption and hold the key, and cut metadata retention from one year to six months. But the bill still lets the minister issue confidential orders to companies. Signal has threatened to leave Canada if it passes as written, Meta said it would have to “consider” its options, and Google warned of secret surveillance directives. Police and child-protection groups urged senators to pass it quickly; one called the tech threats “a big bluff”. Any Senate amendments would send the bill back to the House of Commons.
stories.why: This is the kind of law that decides whether your messaging apps stay fully encrypted in Canada. The fight mirrors Britain’s clash with Apple, and senators now have to choose between police who say they are falling behind and companies and privacy advocates who say secret orders weaken everyone’s security.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Scheduled, not confirmed: the committee hearings and Tuesday’s clause-by-clause review had not happened when sources were checked. Single-outlet story (CBC).

stories.headline: More Canadian adults now use cannabis daily than drink alcohol daily, a CMAJ study of nearly 100,000 people finds
stories.deck: About 5.7% of adults reported daily or near-daily cannabis use in the 2023–24 Canadian Community Health Survey, compared with 5.2% for alcohol, with young adults driving the gap.
stories.summary: About 5.7% of adults reported daily or near-daily cannabis use in the 2023–24 Canadian Community Health Survey, compared with 5.2% for alcohol, with young adults driving the gap. The study, published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, found daily cannabis use exceeded daily drinking in every age group from 18 to 49, and exceeded daily cigarette smoking among adults under 35, though cigarettes remained the most common daily habit overall at 8.5%. Among women aged 18 to 24, daily cannabis use (6.6%) was about 17 times the rate of daily drinking. Most daily users smoked cannabis rather than using edibles or other forms. “We have to take daily cannabis use pretty seriously,” lead author André McDonald of McMaster University told CBC.
stories.why: Canada was the first major country to fully legalise and market cannabis, so the world watches its data. For young adults the finding is the headline: daily cannabis is now more common than daily drinking among young adults, and most of it is smoked, which carries its own health risks.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: The survey is a one-time snapshot of self-reported use, not proof of a trend over time.

stories.headline: Carney trades jokes with rivals, and a pair of comedians, at the Parliamentary Press Gallery dinner
stories.deck: The prime minister brought out This Hour Has 22 Minutes impersonators of himself and Donald Trump at the annual roast in Ottawa on Saturday, Nov. 21.
stories.summary: The prime minister brought out This Hour Has 22 Minutes impersonators of himself and Donald Trump at the annual roast in Ottawa on Saturday, Nov. 21. “This is a tough room. And I’ve been in the Oval Office,” Mark Carney said, before Mark McKinney came out as Carney and Mark Critch as Trump. Carney also joked about his recent comments on telecom competition. Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour teased him about his travel: “God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa.” Carney left soon after his speech, which the journalist emcees called out on stage; Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre stayed all evening and staged a mock “media bailout” with a bag of money. NDP Leader Avi Lewis needled Carney’s early exit, Bloc Leader Yves-François Blanchet paid tribute to independent journalism, and new Green Leader Mike Morrice closed the night.
stories.why: The dinner is a rare night when Canadian leaders are expected to laugh at themselves, and the jokes often point at real weak spots: here, Carney’s frequent trips abroad and his relationship with the press. For anyone interested in comedy and performance, it also shows how much political image now depends on timing and delivery.

stories.headline: Record 98.8% turnout in Hong Kong’s small-circle Election Committee race, with surprise losses for some establishment figures; Beijing hails “healthy competition”
stories.deck: Only 5,709 people were eligible to vote on Sunday, Nov. 22, for the body that will choose Hong Kong’s next chief executive; 5,640 cast ballots, officials said.
stories.summary: Only 5,709 people were eligible to vote on Sunday, Nov. 22, for the body that will choose Hong Kong’s next chief executive; 5,640 cast ballots, officials said, for 723 contested seats across 31 subsectors, with 856 candidates. Hong Kong has about 4.1 million registered voters overall. Together with uncontested, ex-officio and designated seats, the winners form the 1,500-member Election Committee, which will pick the chief executive next year and elect 40 of the 90 lawmakers in 2029. Winners included former justice secretary Rimsky Yuen, Richard Li and Daryl Ng, but Law Society president Roden Tong and General Chamber of Commerce chief executive Patrick Yeung lost, Hong Kong Free Press reported. Chief Executive John Lee called it “healthy competition among patriots”, and on Monday, Nov. 23, Beijing’s Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office said it showed the “fair competition of the new electoral system”. It was the second such race since Beijing’s 2021 overhaul to ensure only “patriots” govern; critics note much of the former opposition is jailed, in exile or has quit politics.
stories.why: This tiny electorate, not the public, decides who leads Hong Kong. Record turnout among a few thousand pre-vetted voters says little about public opinion, but the upsets hint at competition within the pro-Beijing camp ahead of next year’s leadership contest.

PolyU told Hong Kong Free Press only that the venue applicant had cancelled the booking. The blaze on Nov. 26, 2025, started in one residential block under renovation, spread to seven others and killed 168 people, including 10 domestic workers. HKFP reported that some organisers of anniversary events appear to have faced pressure: police reportedly questioned two Catholic churches about planned memorial masses. Chief Secretary Eric Chan said on Nov. 20 that the government “definitely allows” legal memorial activities but warned people not to be used by those “with ulterior motives”.
stories.why: As the first anniversary approaches on Nov. 26, how Hong Kong lets people grieve in public has become a sensitive political question. Migrant domestic workers were among the victims and are often the least heard; losing this event removes one of the few spaces for their stories.

Run by three generations of the Chan family, the brewer is known for locally made dark soy sauce, black vinegar and sweet soybean paste, made with traditional open-air fermentation under the sun. Its site lies in the 447-hectare Kwu Tung North development area, planned for housing, commercial space and a new MTR station within the Northern Metropolis, which aims to turn about a third of Hong Kong’s land into a tech hub closer to the mainland. stories.headline: China says it sentenced a ministry official to death for selling more than 100 intelligence reports to a foreign spy agency
stories.deck: A WeChat account linked to China’s state-secrets watchdog said an official surnamed Ma was recruited while posted abroad and paid more than 1 million yuan.
stories.summary: A WeChat account linked to China’s state-secrets watchdog said an official surnamed Ma was recruited while posted abroad and paid more than 1 million yuan. According to the post on Monday, Nov. 23, on the Baomiguan account, Ma befriended a foreign intelligence officer who first asked about Chinese institutions abroad, then was introduced to a second officer who threatened to report his past wrongdoing unless he cooperated. He signed a cooperation document, received a monthly payment and a dedicated laptop, and kept passing classified material after returning to China, collecting documents at work by day and sending them at night. He was sentenced to death for espionage, stripped of political rights for life and had his property confiscated. The post did not name his ministry, the foreign country, the court or when the case took place.
stories.why: Beijing increasingly publicises spy cases as warnings to its huge bureaucracy, and a death sentence is meant to be noticed. The vagueness is typical: without the ministry, court or country, the case cannot be checked independently, but it signals how seriously China is treating foreign intelligence work as tensions with the West continue.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported
stories.note: The case details come only from an official Chinese secrecy-education account, as reported by Singapore outlets; they cannot be independently verified.

stories.deck: China’s Commerce Ministry said on Sunday, Nov. 22, the U.S. regulator had “overstretched the concept of national security” and that China would take “necessary measures”.
stories.summary: China’s Commerce Ministry said on Sunday, Nov. 22, the U.S. regulator had “overstretched the concept of national security” and that China would take “necessary measures”. The Federal Communications Commission voted on Thursday, Nov. 19, hours after Donald Trump’s talks with Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, to bar China Mobile, China Telecom, China Unicom and other providers on its national-security “covered list” from getting U.S. phone numbers directly for internet-based calling services. The FCC said the rules add security certifications and help fight scam robocalls. A ministry spokesperson said the move breaks the “important consensus” reached by the two presidents and undermines stable trade ties, according to Xinhua as carried by RTHK. The FCC had already barred the three state-owned carriers from providing international telecom services in the U.S. several years ago.
stories.why: Days after a summit meant to steady U.S.–China relations, the tech decoupling keeps going at the regulatory level. Each such step, on phone numbers, equipment or data centres, invites a Chinese response, and the warning of “necessary measures” suggests Beijing may retaliate.

stories.headline: Zelensky says Ukrainian sea drones sank a Russian warship at a port in Libya; Russia has not commented
stories.deck: Ukraine’s president said seven naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at Benghazi’s naval base on Sunday, Nov. 22, and also hit a Russian cargo ship off the Libyan coast.
stories.summary: Ukraine’s president said seven naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at Benghazi’s naval base on Sunday, Nov. 22, and also hit a Russian cargo ship off the Libyan coast. In a statement on Monday, Nov. 23, Volodymyr Zelensky called it “an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war”, saying a Ka-27 helicopter was also destroyed and that the cargo ship, the Angara, carried weapons. Authorities in eastern Libya said the warship had stopped to refuel on its way back to Russia. The BBC said satellite images from Vantor showed the corvette capsized with only its bow visible; Libya’s eastern health ministry said crew from the cargo ship had been rescued. The UN mission in Libya called for an independent investigation, and eastern Libyan commander Saddam Haftar rejected the use of Libyan territory “as an arena for settling scores”. Moscow had not commented, the BBC and Al Jazeera reported. Separately, Russian strikes on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people overnight into Nov. 23, including 11 in a partly collapsed apartment block in Dymer, according to Ukrainian officials quoted by Al Jazeera.
stories.why: If confirmed, this would be one of Ukraine’s longest-range strikes yet, carried out in the Mediterranean, far from the Black Sea. It shows Kyiv is willing to hit Russian military assets wherever they operate, and it drags Libya, already split between rival governments, further into a war it has no part in. It came a day after a Russia-bound cargo ship was hit in the Gulf of Finland.

stories.note: The sinking and the weapons cargo are Zelensky’s claims; the BBC’s satellite and video checks support a ship being badly damaged and capsized at Benghazi. Russia’s side was not available. Casualty figures for the Kyiv-region strikes were still rising when sources were checked.

stories.headline: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore full diplomatic ties after a three-year rift over eastern Congo’s rebels
stories.deck: Presidents William Ruto and Félix Tshisekedi agreed on Sunday, Nov. 22, to return ambassadors and restore full relations, at a summit in Oyo, Republic of the Congo.
stories.summary: Presidents William Ruto and Félix Tshisekedi agreed on Sunday, Nov. 22, to return ambassadors and restore full relations, at a summit in Oyo, Republic of the Congo, hosted by President Denis Sassou Nguesso with Togo’s Faure Gnassingbé as mediator. Ties soured in 2023, when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting the launch of a rebel alliance that includes M23, recalled its envoy and later refused to accredit Kenya’s ambassador. Tensions grew after Kenya named a consul-general to M23-held Goma and hosted Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025. According to statements from both leaders, they agreed to restore ambassador-level representation, revive a joint cooperation commission and respect each other’s sovereignty and non-interference, and to work together on trade, security and the Ebola outbreak. The BBC noted that more than 5,700 people have died of Ebola in DR Congo since May.
stories.why: Kenya is East Africa’s diplomatic and trade hub, and DR Congo’s war in the east has strained the whole region. Restoring ambassadors does not end the fighting, which the WHO says is disrupting the Ebola response, but it removes one quarrel that had blocked regional mediation.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported
stories.note: The agreement terms come from the two presidents’ own statements as reported by the BBC and Xinhua (Chinese state media). No timetable for returning ambassadors was given.

stories.headline: South Korea’s education minister resigns after chaotic anti-AI-cheating measures at the national college entrance exam
stories.deck: Choi Kyo-jin stepped down on Sunday, Nov. 22, taking responsibility for last-minute rules meant to stop AI-assisted cheating on the Suneung, sat by about 500,000 students.
stories.summary: Choi Kyo-jin stepped down on Sunday, Nov. 22, taking responsibility for last-minute rules meant to stop AI-assisted cheating on the Suneung, sat by about 500,000 students on Thursday, Nov. 19. The measures followed a confession by the top scorer in April’s national tax accountancy exam, who said he photographed questions with a micro-camera, sent them to an AI tool and checked answers on his phone. On exam day, the government sent three nationwide emergency alerts that made phones across the country sound at once, candidates had to cover shirt buttons that could hide cameras, and glasses were inspected; the ministry said 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices. “I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance,” Choi said. President Lee Jae Myung accepted the resignation about an hour later and told Prime Minister Han Seong-sook to oversee follow-up measures, Yonhap reported.
stories.why: For millions of young Koreans the Suneung shapes university and career chances, so trust in it is a national issue. The episode shows how cheap AI tools plus tiny cameras are forcing exam systems everywhere to rethink security, and how heavy-handed fixes can punish honest students too.

stories.headline: Carlos Alcaraz beats world No. 1 Alexander Zverev to win his first ATP Finals title
stories.deck: The 23-year-old Spaniard won 6-2, 7-6 (7) on Sunday, Nov. 22, becoming only the fourth man with a career Grand Slam and an ATP Finals trophy.
stories.summary: The 23-year-old Spaniard won 6-2, 7-6 (7) on Sunday, Nov. 22, becoming only the fourth man with a career Grand Slam and an ATP Finals trophy, after Andre Agassi, Roger Federer and Novak Djokovic. Alcaraz saved three set points in the second-set tiebreak and finished the season on a 14-match winning streak, having also won in Vienna and Paris, despite missing about four and a half months mid-year with a wrist injury and playing the week with a strapped hamstring. Zverev, who won his first two Grand Slam titles this year and reached No. 1 this month, had not dropped a set before the final. “This trophy is something I have been chasing for a really long time,” Alcaraz said. CBC reported his winner’s cheque at almost $5.2 million US.
stories.why: The season-ending event was the one big title missing from Alcaraz’s record. Beating the new world No. 1 so clearly, while carrying injuries, sets up 2027 as a fight over who really leads men’s tennis, with Jannik Sinner returning from a knee injury.
